title: Acts
subtitle: the Spirit-filled witnesses, from Jerusalem to Rome
lead: The Acts of the Apostles tells how a small group of Jesus' followers in Jerusalem became, within about thirty years, a movement of Jews and Gentiles in the great cities of the Roman Empire. It is the second volume of a two-part work: the first, the Gospel of Luke, told "everything Jesus began to do and to teach" (1:1); Acts tells what the risen Jesus went on doing through his apostles and the Holy Spirit. The book begins with Jesus taken up on the Mount of Olives and ends with Paul under guard in Rome, "proclaiming the kingdom of God" without hindrance.

Jesus' last words in Acts give the plan of the whole book: his followers will be his witnesses "in Jerusalem, and in all of Judea and Samaria, and as far as the farthest end of the earth" (1:8). The first half follows Peter and the Jerusalem church; the second follows Paul across Asia Minor, Greece and the sea to Rome. Along the way Acts tells of the gift of the Spirit at Pentecost, the first martyr Stephen, the call of Saul, the welcome of Gentiles without circumcision, and the long, painful debate among Jews over whether Jesus was Israel's Messiah. It is our main source for the history of the earliest church, and it is still read by every Christian tradition as a guide to what the church is meant to be.
facts: Anonymous. From the late 100s the church named Luke, "the beloved physician" and companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11). Many critical scholars: an unknown admirer of Paul, writing a generation or more later.
Debated: about AD 62 (where the story ends), AD 80–90 (the most common view), or AD 100–120 (a minority, such as Richard Pervo).
From Jerusalem to Rome, about AD 30–62: Judea, Samaria, Syria, Cyprus, Asia Minor, Macedonia, Greece, Crete, Malta and Italy.
An ancient history, in the manner of Greek and Jewish historians, with many speeches. Some scholars call it apologetic history, a biography of the apostles, or a historical novel.
Greek, some of the most polished in the New Testament, with a Bible-like style in the early chapters set in Jerusalem.
authorship: The book never names its author, but its preface links it to Luke's Gospel (1:1; Luke 1:1–4). Irenaeus, about AD 180, says that Luke, Paul's companion, wrote the Gospel and was "inseparable" from Paul, and he points to the "we" passages of Acts as proof (Against Heresies 3.1.1; 3.14.1). The Muratorian Fragment (usually dated to the late 100s, though some argue for the 300s) says that Luke the physician wrote "the acts of all the apostles" in one book for "most excellent Theophilus." The so-called Anti-Marcionite Prologue to Luke adds that Luke was a Syrian of Antioch, a doctor, who died unmarried at eighty-four. Paul's letters name Luke as a coworker and "the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11). Many Catholic, Orthodox and evangelical scholars, and some critical ones, accept Luke as the author.

In three stretches the narrator says "we" (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), as if he traveled with Paul from Troas to Philippi, from Philippi to Jerusalem, and from Caesarea to Rome. The traditional view is that the author was there. Others think he used a travel diary written by a companion, or that "we" is a literary device: Vernon Robbins argued that sea-voyage stories were often told in the first person; Richard Pervo, that "we" lends a fictional eyewitness color. Defenders of the traditional view reply that no clear ancient parallel exists for a historian slipping into an unexplained "we."

In 1882 William Hobart argued that Luke-Acts uses many medical terms, proving the author was a doctor. In 1920 Henry Cadbury showed that most of these words were common in educated Greek, in writers such as Josephus and Lucian. Most scholars now say the vocabulary is consistent with a physician but proves nothing (see the note at 3:7).

Many critical scholars doubt that a companion of Paul wrote Acts. They point to differences between Acts and Paul's letters: Paul's visits to Jerusalem (Galatians 1–2 and Acts 9, 11, 15), his attitude to the Law, and his theology, which Philipp Vielhauer argued Acts had smoothed into a "Paulinism" Paul would not recognize. They also note that Acts never mentions Paul's letters. Defenders reply that a companion who knew Paul for part of his career, writing years later for his own purposes, would naturally differ in emphasis, and that Acts' accurate local detail (Hemer listed many) points to someone close to the events.

audience.to: Theophilus, called "most excellent" in Luke 1:3, a title used for Roman officials and men of rank, perhaps the book's patron and a believer who had been instructed in the faith (Luke 1:4). Through him the book was written for churches around the Mediterranean, many of them made up mostly of Gentiles, along with Jewish believers and "God-fearers," Gentiles who had worshiped in synagogues. They lived a generation or more after the events, in cities where the movement was small, often misunderstood, sometimes accused before magistrates, and increasingly separated from the synagogues.
audience.why: Luke writes so that Theophilus will know how sure and firm the teaching he received really is (Luke 1:4). Acts answers questions such readers faced. How did a Jewish movement in Jerusalem come to include uncircumcised Gentiles, and was that God's will? Acts shows each step led by the Spirit and approved by the apostles. Is the movement a danger to Rome? Again and again Roman officials find Paul innocent. Has God abandoned Israel? Acts shows thousands of Jews believing and the apostles worshiping in the temple, while also telling of sharp rejection. Knowing this audience explains Luke's choices: the many speeches, the careful notes on Roman officials, the repeated defense of Paul, and the long story of Jewish debate, written for believers who needed to know where they stood in God's story.
views: Some read Acts as political apology: it shows that Christianity is no threat to Roman order, since governors and magistrates (Gallio, Festus, Agrippa) repeatedly declare Paul innocent. Others reply that a Roman official would hardly read a book so full of Jewish Scripture.

Many think Acts defends Paul to Jewish Christians who suspected him of teaching Jews to abandon the Law, by showing him circumcising Timothy, keeping vows and worshiping in the temple (16:3; 21:20–26).
Jacob Jervell and others read Acts as showing that the church of Jews and Gentiles is the restored Israel promised by the prophets, with repentant Israel at its core and Gentiles joined to it.

The Tübingen school of F. C. Baur read Acts as a second-century attempt to reconcile the parties of Peter and of Paul. Few hold Baur's full theory today, but many still see Acts stressing harmony among the apostles.
Others stress pastoral purpose: Acts gives an identity and hope to small, persecuted communities by showing that God's plan, foretold in Scripture, is unstoppable.

outline: Beginnings in Jerusalem: the preface, the ascension, Matthias, Pentecost and the first community
The witness in Jerusalem: healing in the temple, trials before the council, shared life, the Seven, Stephen's speech and death
Judea and Samaria: Philip in Samaria, Simon, the Ethiopian official, Saul's call
The door opens to the Gentiles: Peter and Cornelius, the church at Antioch, Herod Agrippa's death
Paul and Barnabas sent out: Cyprus and Galatia, and the council at Jerusalem
Into Europe: Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens and Corinth
Ephesus and the journey to Jerusalem: Apollos, the riot, the farewell at Miletus
Paul arrested and on trial: Jerusalem and Caesarea, before Felix, Festus and Agrippa
To Rome: storm and shipwreck, Malta, and two years preaching under guard

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Acts against the Roman East of the 30s to 60s: governors, the Herods, cities, inscriptions and archaeology, travel by road and sea, and what can be known of Peter and Paul. Used by historians of every background, from William Ramsay and Colin Hemer to Ernst Haenchen.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the book was made: who wrote it and when, what sources lie behind it (the "we" passages), how Luke composed the speeches, how Acts compares with Paul's letters, how far it is reliable history, and what the longer Western text is.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads Acts as the second half of one story with Luke's Gospel: the outline of 1:8, the summaries of the word's growth, the speeches, the matching careers of Peter and Paul, and the three tellings of Paul's call.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads the early movement as a Jewish group ("the Way," "the sect of the Nazarenes") in the temple and synagogues, with Jewish scholars on Paul and on Acts, and with honest attention to how Acts' "the Jews" was later used against Jews.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: How the fathers, the creeds, the liturgy and the churches have read Acts as a charter for church order, sacraments, mission and councils, from Chrysostom's homilies to the Reformation and Pentecostalism.

sections.b:
Read Acts as volume two. Luke's Gospel moves toward Jerusalem, where Jesus dies and rises; Acts moves out from Jerusalem to the nations. The same patterns appear in both: Jesus and Paul both make a fateful journey to Jerusalem, both are tried before Jewish and Roman authorities, both are declared innocent. Jesus' last words in Acts (1:8) are the book's map: Jerusalem (chapters 1–7), Judea and Samaria (8–9), and the wider world (10–28).

The real main character is the word of God, carried by the Spirit. Six times Luke pauses to report that the word grew or the church multiplied (6:7; 9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20; 28:31), and each summary closes a stage. Despite its title, Acts is not the acts of all the apostles: most of the Twelve disappear after chapter 1, and the book centers on Peter, Stephen, Philip, Barnabas and above all Paul.

About a third of the book is speeches. They are where Luke explains the meaning of events, and each one is shaped for its hearers: Jews in Jerusalem, a Roman officer's household, a synagogue in Galatia, philosophers in Athens, elders of Ephesus, a Roman governor and a Jewish king.

sections.h: What kind of book is it?
sections.b: Ancient readers would have recognized Acts as history, with a formal preface, speeches and attention to dates and officials. But scholars debate which kind. History: most place Acts among Greek and Jewish histories, like those of Thucydides, Polybius or Josephus; Gregory Sterling calls it "apologetic historiography," the story of a people told to define and defend it. Biography: Charles Talbert compared Luke-Acts to ancient lives of philosophers followed by their successors. Novel: Richard Pervo, in Profit with Delight, argued that Acts entertains like an ancient novel, with shipwrecks, prison escapes and riots, and should be read as edifying fiction more than history. Most scholars think Acts uses the techniques of the novel and of rhetoric in the service of history, and that a work can be both theologically driven and historically grounded.

About AD 62: the story ends with Paul still awaiting trial in Rome after two years (28:30). Some argue that Luke wrote at that moment, which is why he does not tell of Paul's death, the fire of Rome in 64, Nero's persecution, or the fall of Jerusalem in 70. Adolf von Harnack came to this view late in life. AD 80–90: most scholars date Acts after Luke's Gospel, which seems to know of Jerusalem's destruction (Luke 21:20), and before Paul's letters were collected and widely known; the open ending is read as deliberate. AD 100–120: Richard Pervo and Joseph Tyson argue that Acts used Josephus' Antiquities (about 94) and Paul's letters, and that it answers second-century debates, such as those raised by Marcion.

Acts and Paul's letters are our two sources for Paul, and they sometimes disagree. Paul says that after his call he went to Arabia and came to Jerusalem only after three years, seeing only Peter and James (Galatians 1:15–20); Acts tells a fuller Jerusalem visit with Barnabas introducing him (9:26–30). Scholars debate whether the Jerusalem meeting of Galatians 2:1–10 is the council of Acts 15 or the famine visit of Acts 11:30. Acts never mentions Paul's letters, and its Paul is more friendly to the Law (16:3; 21:26) than the Paul of Galatians seems. Philipp Vielhauer argued that Acts' theology is not Paul's; others reply that the letters show Paul saying, "To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win Jews" (1 Corinthians 9:20) and that Acts and the letters complement each other more than they conflict. The part pages discuss each place.

Acts survives in two distinct forms more than any other New Testament book. The text in most modern Bibles rests on the oldest Greek manuscripts, such as Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (300s) and early papyri. The "Western" text, best known from Codex Bezae (about AD 400, Greek and Latin on facing pages), with Old Latin and some Syriac witnesses, is about 8.5 percent longer. It adds vivid details (the "seven steps" of the prison, 12:10; Paul teaching "from the fifth hour to the tenth," 19:9), names and explanations, and gives a different form of the apostolic decree (15:20, 29).

How did two texts arise? Friedrich Blass (1895) proposed that Luke himself issued two editions. M.-É. Boismard and A. Lamouille argued for stages of Luke's own work; W. A. Strange, that Luke left an unfinished draft with notes that two editors published differently. Eldon Epp showed that Bezae's changes often have a theological tendency, above all a sharper picture of Jewish hostility; Ben Witherington argued that the Western text also lessens the role of women. Most textual critics, and the Editio Critica Maior of Acts (2017), treat the shorter text as closer to the original and the Western text as an early, free revision. This translation follows the shorter text and gives the Western readings in variant notes where a reader would notice them.

sections.h: Why does Acts end where it does?
sections.b: Acts closes with Paul in Rome, living two years at his own expense under guard, welcoming everyone and preaching "with complete freedom to speak, and no one stopped him" (28:30–31). It does not tell the outcome of his trial or his death, which early tradition places under Nero. Readers have offered several explanations: Luke wrote before Paul's trial ended; Luke planned a third volume; Luke's purpose was complete once the word reached Rome; or the open ending is deliberate, inviting readers to continue the story, and to know, as they did, that the chained apostle's word could not be chained. Many scholars hold the last view, often with the second as a possibility.

Nearly every leading figure in Acts is Jewish, and the movement begins in the temple and the synagogues. Thousands of Jews believe (2:41; 4:4; 21:20), and the believers are called a Jewish "sect" (24:5; 28:22). Yet Acts also tells of repeated conflict with Jewish leaders and synagogues, and its phrase "the Jews" often means opponents. The book ends with Paul quoting Isaiah 6:9–10 to Jewish leaders in Rome and announcing that God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles (28:28). Scholars disagree whether Luke closes the door on Israel (Jack Sanders, Joseph Tyson read Acts as hostile) or keeps it open (Jacob Jervell and others). Later Christians used passages from Acts to blame Jews collectively for Jesus' death. The notes on this site point out where that happened and what the text, in its first setting, actually says.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Acts ends like the history of the kings
spec.body: The great history of Israel in Samuel and Kings ends with a strange, quiet scene: King Jehoiachin, a prisoner in Babylon, is released, given a place at the king's table and an allowance for the rest of his life (2 Kings 25:27–30). Israel's story pauses in the capital of a Gentile empire, with David's heir alive but not free, and the reader left to hope. Acts ends in a similar way: Paul, prisoner in the imperial capital, lives in his own rented quarters under guard, welcomes all who come and proclaims the kingdom of God "unhindered" (28:30–31). I suggest that Luke, who knew Israel's Scriptures closely, shaped his ending on that model: a closing scene of restraint and hope in a Gentile capital, which tells readers that God's story is not finished. Commentators have long discussed the open ending, and some compare it with other ancient endings; the specific link to the end of 2 Kings is my own proposal.

traditions.q: Acts shows apostles, the Seven (6:1–6), elders appointed in each church (14:23), a council of apostles and elders (15:6) and elders called overseers (20:17, 28). What church order, if any, does it make binding?
views: Christ gave his church a hierarchy: bishops, successors of the apostles, with priests and deacons. The laying on of hands in Acts (6:6; 13:3; 14:23) is the root of the sacrament of holy orders, and the Jerusalem council is the model of later councils (Catechism 1536–1538, 1555–1556, 884).

The threefold order of bishop, priest and deacon goes back to the apostles; the bishop is the center of each local church, and councils, as in Acts 15, decide for the whole church guided by the Spirit, whose decision "seemed good" to the Spirit and to the apostles and elders together (15:28).

"From the Apostles' time there have been these Orders of Ministers in Christ's Church; Bishops, Priests, and Deacons" (Preface to the Ordinal), which the Church of England keeps, while allowing that Scripture does not lay down every detail.

One office of preaching and sacraments was instituted by God; its forms of oversight, including bishops, are human arrangements that may differ, as long as the gospel is purely taught (Augsburg Confession 5, 14, 28).

In the New Testament "elder" and "overseer" name the same office (20:17, 28); churches are to be ruled by elders together, with deacons serving the poor (6:1–6), and by assemblies like the council of Acts 15 (Calvin, Institutes 4.3.8; Presbyterian church order).

Each local church governs itself under Christ; the congregation chooses its leaders, as the whole community chose the Seven (6:3, 5); Scripture gives two offices, pastors (elders, overseers) and deacons (Baptist Faith and Message 6).

reading: Craig S. Keener, Acts: An Exegetical Commentary (4 vols., 2012–2015)
The largest modern commentary, with vast background from the ancient world; argues for Acts' historical reliability.
Joseph A. Fitzmyer, The Acts of the Apostles (Anchor Bible, 1998)
A balanced Catholic scholar's commentary with a full bibliography.
C. K. Barrett, The Acts of the Apostles (ICC, 2 vols., 1994–1998)
Detailed work on the Greek text, careful and critical.
F. F. Bruce, The Acts of the Apostles: Greek Text (3rd ed., 1990)
A classic evangelical commentary strong on history and text.
A leading critical commentary that dates Acts to the early 100s and reads it as edifying history.
Luke Timothy Johnson, The Acts of the Apostles (Sacra Pagina, 1992)
A literary and theological reading, readable and insightful.
Robert C. Tannehill, The Narrative Unity of Luke-Acts (2 vols., 1986–1990)
How the two volumes work as one story.
Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament (2nd ed., 1994)
Its long section on Acts explains the Western text verse by verse.
